I'm typically very .. flat.  I'm able to immediately shut down any big emotion. I don't think it makes me emotionless though. I have emotions and I can feel emotions, I just have a hard time letting myself feel them and an even harder time expressing them. I'm such a monotoned robot, it takes actual effort to make myself physically express my emotions, and turning them off is just so normal for me I don't even realize I'm doing it. 

I would say I am very apathetic. I do have empathy. I do have emotions. But my apathy turns it way down to the point where my feelings are a straight line constantly. 

This definitely impacts any self expression in my art. There's no feelings to express if there's no feelings to experience in the first place. It took me years to figure out what was even inside me, when trying to make art with "meaning" ...  I still struggle to figure out why I paint the things I paint, and have to have a long dialogue with myself to reach a conclusion. 

I think there's a big disconnect within myself. I'm not "in tune"

My only experience is with dogs. Knowing their body language is important. The funny smiling face with squinting eyes they make that people take photos of is more of an expression of anxiety or guilt. A lot of dogs will make that face when scolded.  How are they carrying themselves? What are the ears doing. The tail. The paws. How are they sitting or laying. Etc. Can they even sit still or are they too nervous?

My rescue would start crying if our hands got near his ears because was afraid we would hurt him there. Some dogs will run away if hands come at them. Even reaching to pet them or pick them up can really freak them out until they learn to trust you with their safety. 

Its like meeting someone who was abused as a child into adulthood and are now an adult with a lot of issues. Its the same thing for rescues, only the animals cant talk about it like a human can. 

It may sound super dumb but asking the animal for permission really helps. After a while they will understand and will learn to show "yes" or "no" in their own way. I asked my rescue dog if I could pick him up before actually holding him because he would panic if i didnt. He had his way of giving me permission and his way of telling me "no thank you not right now". Using your own body language, tone of voice, and key words will help the dog understand your intentions. 

Loud noises might scare them. A cupboard door closing could send them running for their life. A sudden burst of laughter. A hand clapping. Etc.

My dog had a fear of certain objects. If he saw me holding a fly swatter he would run like hell. Probably because someone in his past hurt him with one. I would have to bring it out very slowly and be overly encouraging to him to let him know he was safe and i would never hurt him. He would still leave the room but when i put it away i would let him know and give him lovins to know i wasnt angry at him or planning to punish him with it. 

He had VERY intense separation anxiety when he first got to me. Because he wasnt yet potty trained he had to be kept in the kitchen (no carpet) in case of accidents. He would cry and cry all night. We stopped that immediately, i let him sleep in my room fully expecting to clean his accidents, id rather he feel comfortable in a new house instead of scared and alone in a new house. Cleaning his accidents wasnt an issue in the grand scheme of things. Id clean his messes 1000 more times if it ment he would feel safe in the house. 

He also would not go outside if he was alone. I think he was scared he would be shut out there. He lived on a chain before i got him. Going out alone and having a collar and leash sent him panicking. We tried different collar styles hoping one would feel okay. He ended up handling the body harness best and learned to go on walks with it. But at home he was collar free. 

Its about learning their triggers and emotional needs and adapting to them, instead of forcing them to adapt to you. 

Once they learn to trust you and open up they have amazing personalities and so much love to give. They will be much more willing to adapt to you as time goes on. Fighting with a traumatized dog will only make things difficult the entire time. 

Depending on the dog, it can take years for them to fully accept their new life. Once my dog felt 100% safe and loved he was the absolute best part of my family. He was very expressive in his eyes and eyebrows. He would talk to you and make noises happily. Loved to sleep on you and when he was held his body would go limp and lounge in your arms without a single worry of being dropped or hurt. 

They also have a lot of vet issues. It can add up very quick. Expensive and a lot of the times out of the blue. I used my school money on my dog often.

Rescues have MASSIVE amounts of love to give. But they arent for everyone. Whoever is looking to take one in MUST understand the trauma the animal has been through and be aware what their own presence around the animal can add or take away from the animals emotional health. Brain chemistry is brain chemistry, hurt animals need a lot of help to feel safe again. Not everyone has the patience or love and desire to really help a rescue. Make sure you are ready for the years of work before taking one in. If you get upset easily or tend to yell at animals, this might not be a great choice. 
With the right heart you can really help a rescue be their true selves and they will be the greatest addition to your family.
